Gastrointestinal Disorders

Acute Appendicitis

Appendicitis is common, time-sensitive, and easy to miss when the presentation is early, atypical, pregnant, pediatric, older, or competing with GU/GYN disease. The ED job is to combine serial abdominal exam, pregnancy-aware differential, labs, imaging strategy, and early surgical consultation.

Board trap: Normal WBC or partial pain improvement does not exclude appendicitis; delayed diagnosis raises perforation and litigation risk.

ACUTE APPENDICITIS

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Acute appendicitis is a leading surgical cause of abdominal pain. It can occur at any age, but diagnostic delay is most dangerous in young children, older adults, pregnancy, and patients with barriers to follow-up. The historical pattern is helpful but not mandatory.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Luminal obstruction increases intraluminal pressure, venous congestion, bacterial overgrowth, ischemia, transmural inflammation, and eventually perforation or abscess. The progression explains why early uncomplicated disease may be subtle but complicated disease becomes systemic and peritoneal.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Typical symptoms include vague periumbilical pain that migrates to the RLQ, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fever, and pain worsened by movement. Exam may show McBurney tenderness, guarding, rebound, Rovsing, psoas, or obturator signs. Rosen quantifies that symptoms and maneuvers shift probability rather than prove disease.

DIAGNOSIS

The diagnosis remains clinical plus adjunctive testing. The differential is broad across GI, GU, GYN, and musculoskeletal causes; reproductive-age patients need pregnancy testing and pelvic/gynecologic consideration when appropriate. A complete physical examination matters because missed torsion, ectopic pregnancy, renal colic, psoas abscess, or inflammatory bowel disease can mimic appendicitis.

SCORING SYSTEMS

Alvarado, Pediatric Appendicitis Score, and Appendicitis Inflammatory Response score can stratify low, intermediate, and high risk. They are useful to organize thinking and guide imaging or consultation, but they do not replace clinician judgment or reassessment.

LABORATORY TESTING

WBC elevation is common but nonspecific; a normal WBC does not rule out appendicitis. CRP may help when combined with WBC and pretest probability, but no single biomarker is definitive. Urinalysis can show microscopic hematuria or pyuria from local irritation. Pregnancy testing is required when pregnancy is possible; BMP, LFTs, lipase, or other tests are guided by alternatives.

IMAGING

Early surgical consultation is reasonable before imaging in straightforward adult cases. Imaging is used when diagnosis is uncertain, the presentation is atypical, perforation/abscess is suspected, or alternative disease must be excluded. Plain radiographs are usually low value, but may show free air, bowel obstruction, or appendicolith in select cases.

Graded-compression ultrasound is the initial modality of choice in children and pregnant patients when available. A noncompressible appendix, diameter usually greater than 6 mm, wall thickening, periappendiceal inflammation, hyperemia, appendicolith, abscess, or free fluid supports diagnosis. CT is highly accurate in adults and alternative diagnosis search; MRI is important in pregnancy and selected pediatric pathways when US is nondiagnostic.

TREATMENT

Patients with suspected appendicitis need early surgical consultation, NPO status, IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and antibiotics when appendicitis is diagnosed or strongly suspected. Antibiotics should cover enteric gram-negative and anaerobic organisms. Analgesia should not be withheld just to preserve the exam.

Antibiotics-only treatment may be feasible for carefully selected uncomplicated appendicitis, but selection is strict and follow-up must be reliable. Complicated appendicitis, appendicolith with high-risk features, systemic illness, immunosuppression, advanced age, abscess, or perforation pushes toward operative/specialty-directed care.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Surgery remains accepted standard care for acute appendicitis. Patients transferred or admitted need serial examination and definitive pathway. A patient with negative or equivocal workup may discharge only if pain is controlled, oral intake/hydration is adequate, follow-up is reliable, and return precautions are explicit. Persistent, worsening, or migrating pain after discharge requires immediate reassessment.

SPECIAL POPULATIONS

Uninsured/underserved, communication barriers, institutionalized patients, and those without consistent medical care may present late and need lower threshold for observation or admission. Pregnant patients need obstetric and surgical coordination, ultrasound-first imaging, and MRI when US is nondiagnostic and available. Children and older adults often present atypically; older adults have higher perforation and morbidity risk.
